title: Should Leaders Be Feared or Liked?
metaTitle: Should Leaders Be Feared or Liked? What Research Shows
metaDescription: The research leans toward warmth plus competence over fear. Fear gets short-term compliance but erodes the trust and candor good teams depend on.
keyFinding: Research leans toward warm-and-competent, respected leadership over fear: fear can buy short-term compliance, but it erodes the trust, candor, and psychological safety that better predict how teams actually perform.
honestAnswer: On the evidence, the framing is a little off — the more useful contrast is not feared versus liked but respected versus merely obeyed, and the research leans clearly toward leaders who are seen as both warm and competent rather than primarily intimidating. Machiavelli's famous line that it is safer to be feared than loved is the popular foil here, and there is a grain of truth in it: fear does reliably produce compliance. But compliance is a much thinner thing than what good teams actually run on.

What the work on how people judge each other, and on what makes teams perform, points to is that warmth — read as trustworthiness and good intent — tends to come first, and that fear-based leadership quietly undermines the conditions, especially candor and psychological safety, that the best teams depend on. So the honest answer is that respected, warm-and-competent leadership generally beats fear; fear can get people to do what they are told, but it tends to cost you the honesty and trust you most need from them.
whatDataShows: People appear to judge others on two main dimensions, and warmth tends to lead. The warmth-competence model developed by Fiske, Cuddy and Glick finds that when we size someone up we ask, roughly in this order, whether they mean us well (warmth) and whether they can act on it (competence). Warmth — trustworthiness, good intent — is typically processed first and weighted heavily, because historically it mattered most to know whether a stranger was friend or threat before judging how capable they were.

Building on that, Amy Cuddy has argued that leaders who establish warmth first earn more trust and, through it, more genuine influence than those who try to lead with toughness or competence alone. The claim is that projecting strength before warmth can read as cold and even threatening, which makes people defensive rather than cooperative — whereas warmth first opens the door for competence to actually land. This is a strong, well-argued position rather than a settled law, but it is consistent with the broader two-dimension research.

The team-level evidence points the same way. Amy Edmondson's research on psychological safety — the shared sense that you can speak up, admit a mistake, or raise a problem without being punished or humiliated — links it to learning and performance, and it was prominent in Google's internal study of what made its teams effective. Fear is more or less the opposite of psychological safety: it teaches people to stay quiet, hide errors, and tell the leader what they want to hear, which is precisely the information environment in which teams underperform.
whyItFeelsDifferent: Fear feels effective because its results are immediate and visible. A frightened team moves fast, hits the deadline, and does not push back — so in the short run a fear-driven leader can look highly competent. The costs, by contrast, are slow and largely invisible: the problem nobody flagged, the mistake nobody admitted until it was expensive, the talented person who quietly disengaged or left. The benefits arrive now and the bill arrives later, which makes fear look better than it is.

The 'feared versus liked' framing also taps a stubborn intuition that warmth and toughness are opposites — that to be respected you must be a bit hard, and that being liked means being soft and easily ignored. The two-dimension research cuts against this: warmth and competence are separate axes, not ends of one line, so a leader can be both genuinely warm and genuinely demanding. Being liked and being respected are not the trade-off they are often assumed to be.

And there is a confusion between fear and respect. They can look similar from the outside — people defer, people comply — but they produce very different behaviour when the leader is not watching. Respect tends to survive bad news and invite honesty; fear tends to produce silence and self-protection. Because the surface looks the same, it is easy for a leader to mistake the compliance fear buys for the trust respect earns.
whatResearchSaysToDo: The most consistent guidance is to establish warmth before leaning on competence or authority. Cuddy's argument is that signalling genuine good intent first — that you are on people's side and can be trusted — is what allows your competence and your demands to be received rather than resisted. That does not mean being permissive; it means people need to believe you mean well before your toughness reads as standards rather than threat.

Deliberately building psychological safety is the team-level version of the same idea. Edmondson's work suggests leaders can foster it by responding to mistakes and bad news with curiosity rather than punishment, inviting dissent and questions explicitly, and admitting their own fallibility — all of which signal that speaking up is safe. The payoff is a team that surfaces problems early, which is hard to overstate the value of.

Pairing warmth with real competence and clear, high standards is what the two-dimension research actually points to — not warmth instead of demands. The combination people respect most is a leader who plainly has their back and plainly expects a lot. Warmth without competence reads as nice but ineffective; competence without warmth reads as capable but cold. The aim is both at once.
whatDoesNotHelp: Leading with toughness or intimidation to establish authority tends to backfire on the very thing it is trying to build. The evidence suggests projecting strength before warmth often reads as cold or threatening and makes people defensive, which buys compliance at the cost of trust, candor, and the willingness to flag problems — the things that actually drive team performance.

Chasing likability for its own sake does not help either, and is a common misreading of the warmth research. Warmth in this literature means trustworthiness and good intent, not avoiding hard conversations or trying to be popular. A leader who is pleasant but will not hold a standard or deliver difficult feedback scores high on warmth and low on competence — which the research says people find likeable but do not deeply respect.

Treating fear as a sustainable strategy because it 'works' confuses short-term compliance with effectiveness. Fear does produce obedience, exactly as Machiavelli suggested — but obedience is not candor, initiative, or honesty, and the team-performance research consistently points to those latter qualities, not mere compliance, as what separates the best teams from the rest.
realNumbersInContext: This is an area where the honest move is to flag that the findings are robust but mostly directional rather than precisely quantified. The warmth-competence model (Fiske, Cuddy and Glick) and Edmondson's psychological-safety research are well-established in social and organisational psychology, and warmth being judged first is one of the more reliable findings about social perception. But translating 'warmth beats fear for leaders' into a single number overstates what the evidence can carry.

It is also worth being fair to the foil. Machiavelli's claim that fear is more dependable than love is not simply wrong — fear genuinely does produce reliable short-term compliance, which is part of why the approach persists. What the modern research adds is the part of the ledger he could not measure: the slow erosion of trust, candor and psychological safety that fear tends to cause, and the link between those qualities and how teams perform over time. The verdict is a lean, not a certainty: respected, warm-and-competent leadership generally outperforms fear.

faqs.question: Is it better for a leader to be feared or liked?
faqs.answer: The research leans toward neither extreme: the strongest position is being respected as both warm and competent. Fear reliably produces short-term compliance but erodes trust, candor and psychological safety, which better predict team performance. Being liked for warmth without competence earns affection but not deep respect.

faqs.question: What is the warmth-competence model?
faqs.answer: It is a framework from Fiske, Cuddy and Glick describing two main dimensions on which people judge others: warmth (trustworthiness and intent) and competence (ability). Warmth is usually judged first and weighted heavily, because knowing whether someone means you well historically mattered before knowing how capable they were.

faqs.question: Doesn't fear get results?
faqs.answer: In the short term, yes — fear reliably produces compliance, which is the grain of truth in Machiavelli's 'better to be feared.' But compliance is thinner than candor, initiative and honesty. Fear tends to teach people to stay quiet and hide problems, which is the opposite of the psychological safety linked to high-performing teams.

faqs.question: What is psychological safety and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: Coined in this context by Amy Edmondson, it is the shared belief that you can speak up, admit a mistake, or raise a concern without being punished or humiliated. Her research links it to learning and performance, and it featured prominently in Google's study of what made its teams effective.

faqs.question: Does being warm mean being soft or permissive?
faqs.answer: No. In this research warmth means trustworthiness and good intent, not avoiding hard conversations. Warmth and competence are separate dimensions, so a leader can be both genuinely warm and genuinely demanding. The combination people respect most is someone who clearly has their back and clearly expects a lot.

dataSources: Fiske, S. T., Cuddy, A. J. C., & Glick, P. — the warmth-competence model of social perception (warmth judged before competence).
Cuddy, A. J. C. — work on warmth-first leadership and why projecting warmth before strength builds trust and influence.
Edmondson, A. C. — research on psychological safety and its link to team learning and performance.
Machiavelli, N., The Prince — the 'better to be feared than loved' position, cited here as the popular foil.
